newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Seed oils may regain market share from tropicals.
newsitem.headline: Seed oils may regain market share from tropicals.

text.p: Edible oils supply from annual crops may claw back lost market share from tropical oils from traditionally cheaper tree crops, said James Fry, managing director of researchers Landell Mills Commodities.

"Perennial crops have been gaining output and trade share for 15 years but producers will need to defend this share against the background of rising wage costs in south east Asia," he told the Lipidex 97 oilseeds conference.
"Producers of annual crops will mechanise production and gain from the use of genetically altered varieties."
"In the medium term, tree crops will lose ground to vegetable oils unless producers find ways to reduce labour usage and harness the potential of genetic modification."
Especially palm oil from Malaysia and Indonesia has been rapidly gaining share of global oil output and of the trade volume of oils used in such areas as margarine and cooking fats.
Palm oil in 1964 accounted for 16 percent of total output of the four main oils, soy oil, palm oil, rapeseed oil and sunseed oil, but it is now in second position at 30 percent.
The other three are from annual crops grown in Europe and the Americas.
Palm oil is the most heavily traded of the oils, with 69 percent of output exported versus 35 percent of soy oil.
Landell Mills (LMC) figures show estimated 1996/97 output of palm oil at 16.37 million tonnes, soy oil at 20.39, rape oil at 10.38 and sun oil at 8.65 million tonnes.
The corresponding 95/96 figures for the four commodities were 15.48 million, 20.08, 11.14, and 8.77.
The remainder of the 69.09 million 96/97 global oil output total was made up of groundnut and cotton oils as well as the other tropical oils -- coconut and palm kernel oil.
Fry said actual production costs of all vegetable oils were declining mostly due to yield improvements while prices were developing in response to expanding global demand.
Palm oil prices were usually well below the world market average while soy and coconut oil followed it closely and sun and rape oil were often above it.

However, inflation-adjusted palm oil production costs had been levelling off since 1987 as wages rose faster than in competing industrialised countries, which eroded the potential advantage of year-round harvesting.
While genetic modification has so far generated chances to save herbicide costs and raise yields of soybeans and rapeseed, tropical oil producers still needed to discover this potential.
They must also find better manpower uses in the cultivation and harvesting of fresh fruit bunches at a time that annual crop farmers were cutting costs with rising mechanisation.
Within the palm oil sector, Malaysia's prime position would come under challenge from Indonesia, where costs are lower.
But this would not be quickly felt in export markets as Malaysia's export rate of 55 percent of output compared with 17 percent in Indonesia, where more oil was consumed domestically.
Malaysia in 96/97 should produce 8.40 million tonnes of palm oil, 3.7 percent more than in 95/96 and Indonesia 4.89 million, 7.9 percent more, LMC figures show.
